claims.text: The initial material is a cast, coarse-grained FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy produced without cobalt.
In situ high-temperature tensile testing combined with synchrotron X-ray diffraction and EBSD can uncover deformation mechanisms in FeNiCrMn.
Elevated-temperature deformation of FeNiCrMn exhibits enhanced dislocation glide.
Elevated-temperature deformation of FeNiCrMn exhibits modest or low levels of twinning.
The elevated-temperature deformation mechanisms correlate with increased work-hardening and improved ductility relative to room-temperature post-mortem results.
The proposed testing protocol spans room temperature through approximately 600–800 °C under an inert atmosphere and quasi-static strain rates.
Changes in diffraction peak intensities and broadening reflect dislocation motion and possible twin formation during deformation.
Evolution of grain orientations and morphology reflects dynamic microstructural adjustment during deformation.
Elevated temperature facilitates dislocation glide in FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation glide and possible twinning promote dynamic grain refinement.
Dislocation glide and possible twinning promote internal strain redistribution.
Dynamic grain refinement and internal strain redistribution improve work-hardening and ductility.
Work-hardening rates will increase markedly at elevated temperatures relative to room-temperature benchmarks.
Ductility will increase markedly at elevated temperatures relative to room-temperature benchmarks.
In situ testing will reveal grain reorientation and dislocation activity that are absent from traditional ex situ post-mortem analyses.
Traditional ex situ mechanical testing has not captured real-time microstructural evolution during elevated-temperature deformation.
The observed behavior may differ under high strain rates, cyclic loading, or corrosive conditions.
